statement: The numbers 1, 2, 3, ... fill a grid along diagonals. Diagonal 1 is just 1 (row 1, column 1). Diagonal 2 holds 2 (row 1, column 2) then 3 (row 2, column 1). Each new diagonal is one longer, starts in row 1 and runs down to column 1. Which number is in row 3, column 5?

choices.misconception: I stepped down the diagonal three times from row 1 instead of twice, so I landed in row 4.
I went along the diagonal from the bottom, starting at column 1, instead of starting from row 1.
I gave the last number on that diagonal, the one in column 1, instead of the one in row 3.
I thought row 3, column 5 is on diagonal 8, because 3 + 5 = 8, so I started from 29.

hints: Every square on one diagonal has the same row + column. Work out which diagonal row 3, column 5 lies on, find the number that starts that diagonal in row 1, then step down the diagonal to row 3.
Row + column is 2 on diagonal 1, 3 on diagonal 2, and so on, so row 3, column 5 is on diagonal 7. Diagonals 1 to 6 use 1 + 2 + ... + 6 = 21 numbers.

solutions.reliable: On diagonal 1 the row plus the column is 2, on diagonal 2 it is 3, and so on, so row 3, column 5 (3 + 5 = 8) is on diagonal 7. Diagonals 1 to 6 hold 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 = 21 numbers, so diagonal 7 starts with 22 in row 1, column 7. Going down it, 23 is in row 2, column 6 and 24 is in row 3, column 5. The transferable idea: in a grid filled by a rule, find something that stays the same along the path of the filling, here row + column, and use it to locate a square without drawing the whole grid.

whyOnTest: Grid patterns test whether you find the rule that locates a square, here row + column naming the diagonal, instead of drawing the whole grid.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
